name: The Causal Theory of Reference
statement: A name refers to its bearer through a chain of use tracing back to a first naming, not a description.
statementAccent: a chain of use tracing back to a first naming
meaning: The causal theory of reference, also called the causal-historical theory, holds that the reference of a name, and of natural kind terms, is fixed and transmitted not by an associated description or cluster of descriptions in the speaker's mind but by a causal chain of communication linking the current use of the term back to an original naming event. This is opposed to descriptivism, the Frege-Russell tradition on which a name refers to whatever object uniquely satisfies the description a speaker associates with it. On the causal picture, associated with Saul Kripke's Naming and Necessity, delivered as lectures in 1970 and published in 1972 and as a book in 1980, and with Keith Donnellan, an object is first given its name in an initial baptism, either by pointing to it or by fixing the reference with a description; the name is then passed from speaker to speaker along a chain of communication, each speaker intending to use the name to refer to whatever the person from whom they learned it referred to. A later speaker can thus refer to the object even while associating with the name no uniquely identifying, correct description. Hilary Putnam extended a similar causal and externalist account to natural kind terms such as water and gold. Kripke's arguments overturned the descriptivist orthodoxy and are central to direct reference, rigid designation, the necessary a posteriori, and semantic externalism.
mechanism: The causal theory explains reference by history rather than by descriptive fit. Reference begins with an initial baptism: an object is dubbed with a name, either ostensively, by perceiving and pointing to it, or by a reference-fixing description used only to single it out at the start. Thereafter the name is passed from speaker to speaker in ordinary communication, and each new user acquires the referential intention to use the name for the same thing the person they learned it from used it for. Reference is therefore carried along the causal chain of uses, so a speaker at the far end can refer to the original object even if they know almost nothing accurate about it. Kripke argued against descriptivism with several considerations. The modal argument turns on rigid designation: a name refers to the same object in every possible world, whereas the description a speaker associates with it does not, so the two cannot be synonymous; Aristotle still names Aristotle even in a world where he never taught Alexander. The semantic and epistemic arguments show that reference can succeed with a false or misattributed description: in the Godel case, if it turned out that the incompleteness of arithmetic was actually proved by a man named Schmidt, the name Godel would still refer to Godel, not to whoever fits the man who proved the incompleteness of arithmetic, and in the Feynman case a speaker who knows only that Feynman is a physicist, unable to distinguish him from other physicists, still refers to Feynman. In each case the associated description does not determine the referent, which is fixed instead by the causal-historical chain.

examples.text: An object is named in an initial baptism, and the name is passed along a chain of speakers who intend the same reference.
If Schmidt really proved arithmetic's incompleteness, Godel would still refer to Godel, not to whoever fits the description.
A speaker who knows only that Feynman is a physicist still refers to Feynman, with no uniquely identifying description.

variants.name: Natural kind terms

whyItMatters: The causal theory of reference reshaped the philosophy of language by overturning the long-dominant descriptivist orthodoxy of Frege and Russell, on which names function as disguised descriptions. Kripke's Naming and Necessity is one of the most influential works of twentieth-century philosophy, and its arguments, that names are rigid designators, that reference can succeed without any correct identifying description, and that reference is carried by a causal-historical chain, changed how philosophers think about names, meaning, and the relation between language and the world. The theory has far-reaching consequences: it underwrites the notion of rigid designation, supports the surprising category of the necessary a posteriori, illustrated by Hesperus is Phosphorus and water is H2O, and, extended by Putnam to natural kind terms, grounds semantic externalism, the view that meanings depend partly on the environment and are not fixed by what is in the head. By locating reference in a public, historical process rather than in the private descriptive knowledge of individual speakers, the causal theory reconnected the study of meaning to the social and causal setting of language use. As the account of how names hook onto their bearers through chains of use, it is a landmark in the philosophy of language.

working.text: fix the reference of a name in an initial dubbing, by ostension or a reference-fixing description.
transmit the name through a chain of speakers, each intending the reference of the one they learned it from.
let a speaker refer to the bearer via the causal chain even with no correct identifying description.

limits: The causal theory faces genuine difficulties, several concerning the details of baptism and transmission. The qua problem asks, when an object is baptized by ostension, which thing or kind is actually named, since a single act of pointing is compatible with naming the individual, its stuff, its species, or a part, and the causal theory needs some way to determine what the baptism fixes. Reference change over time is a challenge, since the referent of a name can shift along a chain in ways a purely causal story struggles to capture, and empty names, which have no bearer to be baptized, are awkward for a theory that grounds reference in a causal link to an object. Many now think descriptions play some role after all, at least in fixing reference at the initial baptism, suggesting a hybrid rather than a purely causal account. There are also problems about multiple bearers of the same name. Some of these objections, such as the qua problem, are standard in the literature but should be attributed to it rather than to any single encyclopedia entry, and datings of Naming and Necessity, lectures in 1970, publication in 1972 and 1980, reward care. So the causal theory robustly grounds reference in causal-historical chains, understood as a landmark account challenged by the qua problem, reference change, empty names, and the residual role of descriptions.
misreadings: The causal theory does not claim speakers must know the causal history of a name; it claims that history, not the speaker's descriptions, determines reference. It does not say descriptions play no role at all, since a reference-fixing description may be used in the initial baptism, only that a name is not synonymous with a description. And rigid designation does not mean a name refers to something necessarily existing, only that it refers to the same thing across possible worlds where that thing exists, so treating the theory as requiring knowledge of the chain, as banishing descriptions entirely, or as claiming necessary existence, misreads it.
origin: The account, developed in Saul Kripke's Naming and Necessity (1970, 1980) and by Keith Donnellan and Hilary Putnam, that the reference of names and natural kind terms is fixed by an initial baptism and transmitted along a causal-historical chain rather than by descriptions.
